title: Scaling and Short-Channel Effects
intro: Shrinking transistors changes more than their size: it changes what circuits can do.

blocks.text: In ideal constant-field scaling every dimension and voltage is divided by S (>1) and doping is multiplied by S. Gate delay falls as 1/S, device area as 1/S^2, power per gate as 1/S^2 and power density stays constant. In practice voltages scaled more slowly, which raised power density.

items: Velocity saturation: carriers reach a maximum speed, so ID is nearly linear in Vov at high field.
DIBL: the drain voltage lowers the barrier, reducing VTH and ro.
Mobility degradation: the vertical field reduces mobility.
Hot carriers and gate leakage: reliability and static current.
Narrow-width and well-proximity effects change VTH with layout.

blocks.text: Foundries supply BSIM-family compact models fitted to measurements. Because the process varies, circuits are simulated across process corners: typical (TT), fast (FF), slow (SS) and the skewed corners FS and SF, together with supply and temperature extremes.

blocks.title: Scaling
blocks.text: Technology is scaled by S = 1.4. The old gate length is 180 nm. Find the new length, the relative gate delay, and the relative power per gate.

blocks.title: Why corners?
blocks.text: Give two reasons an analog design must be simulated at process corners.
solution: Device parameters such as VTH, mobility and capacitance vary from lot to lot, shifting bias currents, gm and gain. A circuit that works in TT may lose headroom, bandwidth or phase margin in SS or FF corners, so each specification must hold at all of them (and over supply and temperature).
blocks.answer: Parameter spread shifts bias and speed; specs must hold in all corners.
